articles.title: Don’t derail the transition
articles.content: PAKISTAN has reached astaff-level agreementwith the IMF after completing the fourth review under its programme. Implementation of the Extended Fund Facility is on track, with progress on macroeconomic stability. The challenge is to translate the gains into sustained growth. Political and administrative disruptions that can derail this difficult transition must be avoided. The fiscal deficit has been contained at 2.6 per cent of GDP. The primary surplus has strengthened, supported by provincial cash surpluses and exceptional grants to the federal budget. Revenue targets have been met, though raising petroleum levies amid rising global prices adds to inflationary pressure. The external current account has been broadly balanced, largely because of stronger-than-expected workers’ remittances, despite declining merchandise exports. Sovereign credit ratings have improved, though remaining below 2006-07 levels. Access to global capital markets for long-term financing stands restored, and diversification into instruments like Panda bonds has begun. Foreign portfolio inflows have recovered, but FDI remains disappointing. Talks with the US Treasury on a proposed 10-year Exchange Stabilisation Facility continue, while tariff reduction discussions with the US Trade Representative remain inconclusive. Foreign exchange reserves accumulated by purchasing dollars from the intermarket rather than borrowing now cover three months of imports, up from a trough of $4.3 billion in FY2023, helping stabilise the exchange rate and strengthen the balance of payments. External public debt has declined to 25pc of GDP; the share of short-term debt has fallen from 24 to 16pc, partly after a Saudi deposit was converted into a three-year facility. Yet ordinary citizens see little improvement. Poverty, joblessness, poor public services, unfair taxation, intrusive regulation, and high energy prices constrain households and businesses. Savings and investment are weak, and exports lack the dynamism to sustain growth. We must expand productive capacity, employment, and exports without reigniting inflation or destabilising the external account. This requires completing the structural reform agenda. Federal and provincial governments must be right-sized, civil services professionalised through specialist recruitment and better incentives, and public administration digitised. The FBR must broaden the tax base instead of burdening compliant taxpayers; provinces must effectively implement agriculture income and property taxes. Energy and wheat markets must be made more competitive, with BISP protection for poor households. Restructuring and privatising SOEs, reforming the Export Facilitation Scheme, implementing theNational Tariff Policy, and expanding financial access for small businesses, farmers, women entrepreneurs, and housing are equally important. Export financing and insurance must reach new exporters. Delays or reversals will weaken investment, employment, and competitiveness, undermining the stability painstakingly achieved. Long-delayed infrastructure projects must advance — the Karachi-PeshawarML-1 railway, the Sukkur-Hyderabad motorway, oil pipeline extensions, oil refinery upgrades, the Quetta-Zhob highway, five special industrial zones, and revamping theKarachi Circular Railway. Skills upgrading must complement these investments. Pakistan is midway from crisis management to sustainable growth. Industrial, automobile, and strategic trade policies must be harmonised in consultation with the private sector and announced without delay. A credible implementation framework with clear milestones, assigned duties, and firm timelines is needed. Regular monitoring, inter-agency coordination, and timely bottleneck removal must replace announcements without execution. External risks make the transition more urgent. TheUS-Iran war, disruptions to energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, and instability in Bab el-Mandeb can sharply raise import costs, intensifying uncertainty over inflation, the current account and exchange rate. Suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty compounds water insecurity. Meanwhile, AI is transforming labour markets, creating uncertainty about job opportunities. Against this backdrop, three domestic sources of disruption demand particular attention. First, security in KP and Balochistan must be restored through dialogue and an effective counterterrorism strategy. Poverty and conflict reinforce each other. Reversals in poverty reduction are linked to conflict-affected districts, where social indicators are among the weakest nationally. The NFC framework should give greater weight to disadvantaged districts, alongside empowered local governments (LGs). Federal and provincial governments must jointly own a practical CT plan. The apex committees set up after 2014 showed the value of coordinated action in restoring peace. Imposing emergency and governor’s rule in KP could, instead, intensify political tensions and worsen law and order amid terrorist attacks. Economic relief, jobs, and better public services must complement security operations. Second, the movement of goods and services across the country must be uninterrupted. LEAs requisitioning containers, trucks, and oil tankers disrupt trade. Imports must reach factories on schedule, exporters must honour delivery commitments, and farmers must transport perishable produce to urban markets without delay. Supply disruptions raise prices and create household shortages. Internet shutdowns are equally damaging, disrupting payments, business transactions, logistics, information flows, and the work of freelancers and firms exporting IT and IT-enabled services. Economic activity requires predictable rules and uninterrupted movement of goods, people, and information. Administrative measures intended to address immediate security concerns must not impose disproportionate costs on the economy. Third, the debate over new provinces/ administrative units shouldn’t become another source of instability. It’s a contentious proposal; the Sindh Assembly has opposed dividing the province. Administrative reorganisation requires constitutional clarity, fiscal assessment, and political consensus. Failing to do so would divert scarce resources to new bureaucracies, increase administrative expenditure, and weaken provincial cash surpluses transferred to the centre. Fiscal consolidation will then suffer, jeopardising macroeconomic stability. Strengthening LGs and improving service delivery within existing arrangements should take precedence. Pakistan is midway through a demanding transition from crisis management to sustainable growth. Political leaders hope that the present IMF programme will be the country’s last. Fulfilling that aim needs continuity, discipline, and determined implementation. External shocks can’t be controlled, but their impact can be mitigated through sound policies and domestic consensus. The priority is clear: restore peace through dialogue, keep goods and services moving, complete reforms already initiated, and avoid divisive experiments. Pakistan can’t afford to squander its hard-won stability through preventable disruptions. The transition to growth must be protected, not derailed. The writer is a former State Bank governor.
articles.author: Ishrat Husain

articles.title: Provinces under fire
articles.content: THEliquidationof the KP Assembly is an event rooted in economic, more specifically fiscal, constraints. For the time being, it is unlikely that the trajectory will continue to the other provinces, but it is worth keeping an eye on the resource envelope available to the state as the primary fount of this event. Here is how it works. Every time the state is faced with a major demand for resources, usually for security-related matters, financial managers point to the NFC Award as the reason why that demand cannot be met. In the middle of the 2010s, for example, the then PML-N government faced a major demand for resources to pay for the military operations underway in the wake of the Army Public School massacre by the TTP. The then finance minister Ishaq Dar had said, in December 2016 for instance, that the government had to spend over Rs300 billion on the security operations since they began. He proposed a cut of seven per cent from the Federal Divisible Pool before provincial shares were calculated, in order to meet the expenses going forward. The next year, Miftah Ismail, the then special assistant to the prime minister on finance, again pointed to the NFC Award and provincial expenditures as the reason why the federal government had to run such a large budget deficit and why demands for releases from the development budget might have to wait. That was in October 2017, when Dar was no longer finance minister. In 2019, prime minister Imran Khan told a rally in Ghotki that the 18th Amendment had bankrupted Pakistan, and his government had no resources left to pay for development or relief after paying for debt servicing, defence and transfers to the provinces under the NFC Award. In 2020, his own information minister was telling TV channels that his government might have to “change the law” on the NFC Awards because its allocations had become unsustainable. In 2024, Miftah Ismail was quoted inDawnas saying that “the federal government is teetering on the brink of bankruptcy while the provinces are flush with cash”. Shortly afterwards, the current Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb was quoted in Washington, where he had gone for the annual IMF and World Bank meetings, as saying that Islamabad would revisit the NFC Award, if the IMF loan was approved, through either expenditure-sharing or incentives for provinces to widen the tax base. Many of these people subsequently took their statements back, or at least added caveats that their government had no intention to “roll back” the NFC. The main reason for the backtracking is that every major political party in the country — the PPP, PML-N and PTI — controlled a province, and none wanted to become a party to any attempt to roll back provincial rights. What began as a search for resources turned into a search for a new political arrangement. But the litany of complaints about the enhanced provincial shares under the last NFC continued. Ahsan Iqbal repeated them last year in Karachi, and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif publicly floated the idea of changing the composition of the divisible pool, perhaps by removing customs duties from it. This remark triggered a little conversation of its own, with some delving into how and why these duties were part of the divisible pool in the first place. All along, almost from the very first year when the empowered provincial government’s scheme went into effect from 2009, blaming them has become the favourite excuse for failure in Islamabad. But the scheme itself, which consists of the 18th Amendment and the NFC Award, endured because of the power of consensus behind it. In recent years, though, with the arrival of the ‘hybrid-plus’ government, the conversation around the federative scheme of empowered provinces has turned more menacing. An attempt was made by the federal authorities, for example, to usurp Sindh’s share of water resources, and a demand for some amount of reverse-flow from the provinces to the centre found concrete form in an MoU signed in the NFC meetings as part of the budget for FY27. An amount of Rs1.04 trillion is supposed to be transferred back to the federal government by three provinces — Punjab, Sindh, and KP — this fiscal year. What began as an economic conversation acquired political and security substance as it rolled through the system. As part of the complaints, questions were raised about what the provinces were doing with the incremental resources flowing their way since 2009. Some demanded to know where we should look for the results. A World Bank report landed in the middle of all this, showing that the bulk of incremental resources was consumed in salaries and other current expenditures, while social indicators showed little to no improvement since the scheme of enhanced provincial powers went into effect. That added fuel to the fire. What began as a search for resources turned into a search for a new political arrangement, with some in government publicly saying a “reset” was coming. It acquired a security dimension as the PTI government was called upon to play its part in the counterterrorism operations in KP. And it fed an opportunistic suggestion for wrapping up the whole system and bringing in“administrative units”to replace provincial governments altogether. Somewhere in all this a perception seems to have taken root that the state’s federative structure is too expensive for a resource-starved country like Pakistan. If the provinces have nothing to show for all the funds they have consumed since their powers and resource commitments were enhanced, why keep them longer, ask the proponents of this thinking. They don’t yet have an alternative structure to propose. But in the months to come, it is likely that the governments of Sindh and Punjab will be asked to grant more space to the federal government in the control of the resources they command. The writer is a business and economy journalist.
articles.author: Khurram Husain

articles.title: Pulling the pin
articles.content: ONE does not need to have Mao Zedong’s eyes to see that “everything under heaven is in utter chaos”. There is no continent in the world (except perhaps his China) where conditions are in the control of its leaders. In France, for example, students in the country’s lycées, or secondary schools, are demonstrating against “long school days, overcrowded classrooms, outdated facilities, and teacher shortages”. The protesters are 15- to 18-year-olds. They are too young to vote. Yet their anger threatens to detract from the presidential election in early 2027, when France decides who is to replace Emmanuel Macron. In South America, countries with valuable natural resources and precious minerals are bracing themselves for a raid by the US. If oil-rich Venezuela can be decapitated overnight, can Brazil, Chile and Argentina be far behind? In Ukraine, an embattled Volodymyr Zelensky finds he has now two adversaries — a determined Vladimir Putin, and a mercurial Donald Trump, who has suggested that the Ukrainians “get a new leader who can make a deal”. The abandonment of Zelensky came a day after Trump agreed to buy diesel from Putin. Historians who will chronicle the decline and fall of Trump’s presidency may do worse than rely upon Edward Gibbon’s memorable analysis: “But the decline of Rome was the natural and inevitable effect of immoderate greatness. Prosperity ripened the principle of decay; the cause of the destruction multiplied with the extent of conquest… . … Instead of inquiring why the Roman Empire was destroyed, we should rather be surprised that it has subsisted for so long.” In and around the Arabian Peninsula, the US-Israel vs Iran conflict has taken a sinister turn. Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan have entered into a defence pact. Saudi petrodollars have linked arms with Türkiye’s armament capacity and Pakistani martial manpower. It is less a tripartite alliance than a pas de trois of death. Few realise that this tripartite pact has inbuilt weaknesses. The three countries are not territorially contiguous. Historians may do worse than rely upon Gibbon’s analysis. This new pact purports to imitate the collective defence clause of Article 5 of Nato, which means that should Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, or Türkiye be individually attacked, the other two will have to spring to the victim’s defence. Türkiye is a card-carrying member of Nato. If it is involved militarily, all other Nato member countries will be bound to ‘defend’ Türkiye, and, therefore, by extension Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. That is the legal theory. Practically, Nato’s selectivity has already been tested during the Ukraine crisis. Even though Nato did not extend the umbrella of membership to Ukraine, it chose to defend Ukraine (a non-Nato country) against Russia. Obviously, Nato members and Trump follow Machiavelli’s precept: “He who has the power is always right.” Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan share some commonalities. Each has a Sunni majority, and all three currently have governments that are intolerant of domestic opposition. Recep Erdogan’s government in 2025 imprisoned his most popular rival — Istanbul’s mayor Ekrem Imamoglu. In 2017, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman ordered the detention of over-rich princes and government ministers in the five-star Ritz-Carlton Hotel in Riyadh, where many were allegedly tortured. In 2018, Saudi dissident Jamal Khashoggi was strangled and dismembered by a squad of 15 Saudis (allegedly on the orders of their crown prince) in the Saudi consulate in Istanbul. And here in our country, a leader and his party members — regardless of gender or age — have been sentenced to imprisonment, without the hope of an amnesty. Our federal government is in opposition with smaller provinces — it has imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in KP. Azad Kashmir has had governments drawn from two Pakistani mainstream political parties. The continuing friction brings to mind these lines from Kahlil Gibran’s poignant poem Pity the Nation: “Pity the nation divided into fragments/ each fragment deeming itself a nation.” Not many leaders have the time nor the wit to read Gibbon’s six-volume work on the Roman Empire, or the Meditations bequeathed by the emperor he admired most — Marcus Aurelius. They should. Core lessons derived from Aurelius point to five signs of a weak mind: ‘Surrendering control to external circumstances; complaining and playing the victim; seeking external validation and obsessing over others’ opinions; letting uncontrolled emotions dictate actions; and resisting the present moment and avoiding duty.’ How many leaders — or even us common folk — would survive such a litmus test? Many regard the chaos prevailing everywhere as deeply ominous in its implications. The pin has been removed from the grenade. It is only a matter of time before a doomsday detonation.
articles.author: F.S. Aijazuddin

articles.title: ‘We killed Laiba’
articles.content: ‘SCUM of the earth’ and ‘fraudster’ sound almost like terms of endearment in his case. He will soon be apprehended. Trial and punishment will follow in due course. However, a little soul-searching will make the ultimate verdict clear — we killed Laiba. As the details of her case continue to emerge, let us not get bogged down in numbers; let us assume that the amounts extorted from the family to secure a job for Laiba’s brother or to obtain admission to a university abroad add up to a significant sum, especially for a family that had to sell its life’s savings to meet the asking price. The gravity of the situation, if not already established, warrants a brief digression. While sitting across from a cardiac surgeon, discussing options for my mother’s treatment, I was struck by the following question: “But would you have to sell stuff to afford the recommended treatment?” Until that day, it hadn’t dawned on me that the doctor must ask this often to include it on his list of questions. The minute you hear about a tragedy like Laiba’s recent death by suicide, you start asking: what are they teaching in universities these days? Even a below-average student should know that a scholarship is meant to remove barriers and let a bright student pursue quality education, regardless of location. It shouldn’t require any money to change hands between the aspirant and agents posing as counsellors and consultants. Here, we are talking about a gold medallist from a well-known university. What was she thinking? Then your stomach twists into a million knots as the reality hits: she was killed in an attempt to get a life. While universities here (in fact, our entire education system) aren’t geared towards teaching life skills and critical thinking, the crisis runs much deeper; a state that fails its citizens isn’t safe. It isn’t safe for life, ‘honour’, or investment. Let me explain. A state that fails its citizens isn’t safe. Not a week passes without a young person asking me to help them land a job. I find myself repeating this: first, I am not connected at all; second, even if I were, a good word doesn’t suffice anymore; people don’t oblige without a bribe. More often than not, I am told, ‘we will manage to pay, somehow’. After they confess their desperation, I challenge them — with a fraction of that money, they can start vending fast food at a street corner, and I offer to stand alongside them for a week if they consider it beneath their dignity or not in keeping with their academic degree. It gets them off my back, but the systemic issues blocking enterprise remain. Dangers to life, limb, and property may be gender-blind, but when it comes to sexual assault, women face a double whammy. They are not just physically more vulnerable, but as unwitting keepers of family honour, they are also expected not to talk about any violation, lest they bring shame upon the family, clan, tribe, etc. We are all responsible for the rot, as sickening attitudes that are making the place unlivable are displayed not only in private but also in public rallies and on national television. From a military dictator defending a man accused of assault on TV to the most popular leader of a political party linking women’s dress to triggering man’s innate baseness, we have heard and ignored it all. Social media is replete with clips of that sorry excuse for a man telling his odious interviewer, “jo pasand agai, utha liya” (‘if we like her, we abduct her’). He remains within the fold of the PPP, which rivals the PTI’s claim to being the ‘most popular party’. This is despite the fact that he continues in his vile ways and appears in another video, pointing to his dog and then to an associate, declaring, “only these two are truly loyal to me”. Men are not immune to physical and emotional violence in this environment, but society does not burden them with the shame that keeps women from seeking help. Men have the luxury of appearing macho or vulnerable when it suits them. A public office holder who regularly hurled threats at the opposition and abused women claimed sexual torture in custody. The prime minister has directed the police chief and the interior minister to immediately apprehend the man whose actions led to Laiba’s tragic death. One wonders whether he and his cabinet spent the rest of the day in meetings to figure out how to portray Pakistan as investment-friendly. Visiting cricketers who won’t get a soft drink refill at a burger joint in their own country receive state guest-level security; entire cities are shuttered to ensure visiting dignitaries’ safety, while they jog in public parks back home. The climate and environment are becoming increasingly uninhabitable by the day. The writer is a poet. His latest publication is a collection of satire essays titled Rindana.
articles.author: Shahzad Sharjeel

articles.title: Lagging behind
articles.content: THE IMF’s latest World Economic OutlookprojectsPakistan’s economy to grow by 3.5pc in the current fiscal year, while average inflation climbs to 9.9pc. The current account is expected to slip into a deficit of 1pc of GDP. This forecast points to an economy that remains vulnerable despite recent gains in macroeconomic stability. The economy expanded by 3.6pc last year. Further slowdown matters for a country with a rapidly increasing population, entrenched poverty, and high unemployment. Growth at this pace will hardly raise incomes meaningfully or absorb new entrants into the labour market. Inflation poses another challenge. After easing to 7.1pc last year, it is forecast to rise sharply, leading to fears of further erosion of purchasing power. For families already squeezed by high energy costs, taxes, and essential expenses, renewed price pressures will undermine any benefits from economic stabilisation. The projected current account deficit signals renewed pressure on foreign exchange earnings. Higher oil prices and shipping disruptions make imports more expensive. Unless exports grow faster and are more diversified, stronger domestic demand could again widen the external gap. The IMF expects unemployment to decline to 6.5pc in FY27 from 6.9pc the previous year. But, in the absence of stronger growth, which can create a sufficient number of jobs, that is hardly of any comfort. It does not establish whether new jobs will be productive, secure or adequately paid. Nor does it show whether employment is expanding fast enough to keep pace with the working-age population. The South Asia region is forecast to grow by 6.4pc in 2026. Pakistan’s 3.5pc projection places it far below the regional average, highlighting our failure to build a sustained growth engine. The global picture is also distressing. The IMF forecasts global growth of 3.1pc in 2026, rising to 3.4pc in 2027. Investment in AI is supporting activity in some economies. Others face higher energy costs, trade disruptions, and tighter financial conditions. Growth is also becoming increasingly uneven. We must prepare for these pressures rather than assume that stabilisation will deliver prosperity. The immediate task is to contain inflation and protect vulnerable households without reviving unsustainable subsidies or excessive demand. For that, the government must shift resources towards productive investment, improve the competitiveness of industry, broaden the tax base and expand export capacity. Better education, skills, and employment opportunities are equally important. These changes require consistent policies, not another short-lived cycle of incentives and concessions. The IMF projections expose the cost of postponing structural reform. An economy growing at 3.5pc, with inflation approaching double digits and a weakening external balance, remains vulnerable to the next shock.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: India voter purge
articles.content: THE purge of millions of voters from India’s electoral rolls has sparked widespread demonstrations, spearheaded by young protesters calling for justice. The Cockroach Janta Party is at the forefront of the movement, while more established opposition parties, such as Congress, are also participating actively. The thread uniting these groups is their suspicion that the Indian election commission has been tinkering with the rolls to benefit the ruling BJP. Earlier this year, the youth-led CJP organised a massive anti-government campaign calling for the resignation of the education minister over exam irregularities. The movement succeeded in ousting the minister, with the youthful energy of its participants catching the BJP government off guard. This time too, India’s rulers have responded with brute force, bundling away thousands of protesters, including Rahul Gandhi and CJP leaders, and cutting off access to the iconic Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi. Around 130m names have been removed from the electoral rolls. The Indian election authorities say the deleted names include voters who have died, relocated, or could not be traced. But the Indian opposition has dismissed this explanation. It is believed that many of the deleted voters were Muslims, as well as those belonging to other marginalised groups. Moreover, media reports say that the Indian election commissioner — whose resignation is being demanded — ignored objections from within the commission to the deletion of such a large number of voters. Such purging of the rolls is in keeping with the BJP regime’s marginalisation of vulnerable groups. It has employed lawfare and dubious means in the past as well to delete Muslim votes; millions have been disenfranchised through the National Register of Citizens. Earlier, the BJP and its Hindutva cohorts could get away with trampling the rights of Indian Muslims. But now, their shenanigans are not working. It appears that India’s other communities are also tired of Hindutva’s empty promises and its attempt to remake India in its own image through fair means and foul. The Sangh Parivar has run out of ideas, and its fantasies about a glorious Hindu past will not buy the people bread, or give them jobs. Hopefully, a fairer order can emerge from the tumult, in which all of India’s communities are treated equally.
articles.author: Editorial
